newsitem.title: USA: Cuba-U.S. stalemate a year after planes downed.
newsitem.headline: Cuba-U.S. stalemate a year after planes downed.

text.p: The downing by Cuban MiG jets of two small U.S. planes flown by Miami-based Cuban exiles a year ago has hardened relations between the two Cold War foes and led to tougher sanctions by the United States that annoyed its allies.
One year after the incident off Cuba, its international reverberations continue to be felt by the U.S. government and Cuban President Fidel Castro.
Four Cuban-Americans were killed. They belonged to Brothers to the Rescue, an anti-Castro group that flew missions over the Florida Straits to find rafters leaving Communist-ruled Cuba.

The downings brought outrage against Cuba. But it also hurt relations between Washington and its main allies by prompting the Helms-Burton Act, which tightened the U.S. economic embargo on Cuba by seeking to punish investors from other countries.
The incident was a victory for hardliners within the Cuban exile community who are seeking nothing short of Castro's ouster and have opposed any rapprochement with Havana.

"We are frozen in place. Relations are worse than they have been since the Cuban missile crisis," said Wayne Smith, former head of the U.S. diplomatic mission in Havana and a senior fellow at the Washington, D.C.-based Centre for International Policy.
Experts said Castro and his foes in exile had become uneasy at the warming of relations between Cuba and the United States, marked by an immigration accord two years ago.
Castro has used the plane downings to crack down on internal dissent and step up his war of rhetoric against the United States, blaming the U.S. embargo for his country's economic woes.
For hardline exiles, worried that the two countries were getting too friendly, it was the tyrant showing his true colours.

"It really threw a cold water bucket on those who were advocating change," said Jaime Suchlicki, a Cuba expert at the University of Miami. "It weakened their argument that Fidel Castro is reasonable, that you can negotiate.
The downing of the two Cessnas led President Bill Clinton to sign the Helms-Burton Act, which was virtually dead due to White House opposition before the incident.
The law allows the U.S. government to punish third country companies benefiting from property confiscated under Castro's 1959 revolution.
The European Union and Canada passed counter-measures and challenged the law before the World Trade Organisation, saying it went beyond U.S. jurisdiction.
Smith called passage of the Helms-Burton law an "utterly stupid" way to react to the plane downings.
"It's a matter of shooting ourselves in the foot. Cuba is of no importance to the United States. Our relations with Canada, Europe and Mexico are of the utmost importance," he said.
However, the incident did lead European countries, which were more tolerant of Castro's government, to begin pressing Cuba on issues of human rights and democracy.
"Europe is coming around on the political question to the position of the United States," said Enrique Baloyra, professor of International Relations at the University of Miami.

Some Cuba observers believe that despite world condemnation and the loss of millions of dollars in foreign investment, Castro views the shootdown as a success because he cares more about his grip on power than about international relations and economics.
"He showed that he was a macho in Cuba," Suchlicki said. "We understand it as a loss economically. But his thinking has to do with power, to continuation of the revolution."
For moderates who advocate a normalisation of relations with Cuba and had seen progress after three decades of high tension, the incident was a dramatic setback.
"Had it not been for this we might have had normalisation in the second Clinton administration. Now that's five, six years down the road," Smith said.
"Other countries will continue to invest in Cuba. Five years down the road, someone in Congress will say 'hey this makes no sense,' and Helms-Burton will be repealed."
